column2: The Danube is the second-longest river in Europe, after the Volga. It flows through much of Central and Southeastern Europe, from the Black Forest in Germany to the Black Sea in Romania. The river passes through or borders ten countries, more than any other river in the world, and its basin drains parts of nine more. Four national capitals lie on its banks: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade. For centuries the Danube served as a frontier of the Roman Empire and later as a trade route linking the German states with the Ottoman lands. Its navigation was regulated by international commissions from the middle of the nineteenth century, and the completion of the Main-Danube Canal in 1992 connected it to the Rhine, creating a continuous waterway from the North Sea to the Black Sea. The river's delta, shared by Romania and Ukraine, is one of the largest wetlands on the continent and was designated a World Heritage Site in 1991. Today the Danube carries freight, supports fisheries and hydroelectric plants, and draws tourists to the cities and vineyards along its course.
